newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pensions, railways recharge French labour tensions.
newsitem.headline: Pensions, railways recharge French labour tensions.

text.p: France's centre-right government faces further tension with trade unions over plans to let private pension funds operate and an overhaul of the railways, amid a heated debate on reducing the retirement age.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons said on Thursday there was no question of delaying a bill to split the railways into an operating company and a new state firm that would own the rail infrastructure, despite a strike call by one trade union.
Pons said he had the backing of most unions for a reform which would spin off 134 billion francs ($24.8 billion) of debts of the SNCF state railways to the new infrastructure company.

"Right now the debate is over. This has gone on for a year. I have met the unions on several occasions. Eight out of eight of them say the situation cannot carry on. Six out of the eight accept the reform," Pons told Europe 1 radio.

The vow to push ahead follows adoption by the National Assembly, or lower house of parliament, on Wednesday of a bill to allow the setting up of private pension funds alongside an increasingly overstretched state retirement benefits system.

The biggest unions have put their ideological differences aside to condemn the legislation on the grounds that incentives for employers to pay into private pension funds for their staff would run down the existing system and discourage pay rises.
Memories of the disruption caused when railway workers went on strike in late 1995 are still vivid.

It remains to be seen whether current tensions, mixed with a lack of morale that has sparked a debate on advancing the retirement age to 55 from 60, will produce an explosive cocktail similar to the one that sparked labour unrest and strikes in 1995.

For most on both sides of the political divide and most of the major unions, retirement at 55 -- favoured by 61 percent of French people in a recent opinion poll -- is ruled out as utopian at a time when an ageing population is already putting the current state finances for pensions under pressure.

One French newspaper said on Thursday an unpublished study by the state social security pensions body, the CNAV, estimated the additional cost of allowing retirement at 55 at 117 billion francs in the next 15 to 20 years.

But, even if generalised earlier retirement is unlikely, there have been sporadic demands to stop working at 50 or 55 following a government agreement in December to allow striking truck drivers to quit at 55.
Six public transport unions have called a one-day strike on January 24 to demand retirement at 55, a benefit already enjoyed by Paris transit authority staff and SNCF train drivers.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe has rejected similar calls by bus drivers in the south-western city of Bordeaux.
A crippling, three-week public sector strike in 1995 started with railworkers opposing a now defunct plan by the government to attack the rail staff's early pension rights.
But it is harder to measure the danger of opposition to the latest plan for a separate infrastructure company.
"We cannot go on like this. We have to haul the SNCF out of this downward (debt) spiral," Pons said. Asked if a strike would prompt him to delay the reform, he said "absolutely not".

The reform is opposed by the Communist-led CGT union and the Socialist CFDT, the first and second largest rail unions, on the grounds that it amounts to a break-up and a precursor to opening France's railways to competition.
But the CFDT failed in a meeting on Wednesday to win backing from other unions for its strike call for January 21, when the bill goes to the Senate. The larger CGT is assessing its own alternatives.

Both unions, as well as the more moderate CGC white-collar union and Christian CFTC union, still hope to get the private pensions bill changed to prevent incentives of tax and social security charge exemptions when the Senate reexamines it on January 30.
But they have yet to decide what course of action to take if they fail. ($1=5.395 French Franc)
